record.title: API Reference — Game & Social Endpoints
record.body:
The service surface behind the games: the Phoenix Game API (REST) and the Nakama social layer (gRPC/HTTP). This is a reference for client and tools engineers; contracts are versioned and analytics events are treated as part of the contract.

Game API (Phoenix, REST)

MethodPathPurpose
GET/api/playersList players
GET/api/player/{player_id}Single player by id
GET/api/player/inventoryPlayer's current inventory
POST/api/player/inventoryUpdate inventory
GET/api/player/statsPlayer stats
GET/api/player/levelsLevel list for the player
POST/api/player/levels/completeRecord a completed level
GET/api/leaderboards/weeklyWeekly leaderboard
GET/api/leaderboards/all-timeAll-time leaderboard
GET/api/season-passSeason pass state
POST/api/season-pass/claimClaim a season-pass reward
GET/api/daily-rewardDaily reward state
GET/api/plague-racePlague Race state
POST/validate-receiptReceipt validation (Domino Node backend, not Phoenix)

Nakama (social)

Accounts, friends, and sessions run through Nakama (gRPC 7349, client API 7350, HTTP 7351). Auth is device/session token; the Game API trusts a validated Nakama session.

RPCPurpose
authenticate_deviceCreate / resume an account
list_friendsSocial graph for gifting / leaderboards
write_storageCloud-save blob (progression backup)

Runtime + deployment: Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix.

Breaking a field means bumping the path version. Never silently repurpose a field the client already reads.

record.title: Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix
record.body:
This page describes the Elixir/Phoenix backend services that sit behind the Harmony Games clients — Domino Delights ("Game of Dominoes"/GoD internally), Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" in-store), and Combo Fighter. The services own authoritative game state, player profiles, quests, and live-ops delivery. For the wider system picture and how these tie into Unity and Nakama, see Architecture Overview; realtime multiplayer and matchmaking are documented separately in Nakama Server Setup & Operations.

Ownership is deliberately thin — a ~16-person studio can't staff a service mesh. One Elixir/Phoenix app for Zombie Match 3D (Domino Delights runs on Node.js/Express with Lambda and DynamoDB), one Aurora cluster, a handful of Fargate tasks. Prefer boring and observable over clever.

Runtime & deployment

All services run as a single Elixir umbrella project, released with mix release and packaged into one container image. We run separate ECS Fargate services off that image (state, profile, quests, live-ops) so we can scale and roll them independently without maintaining separate codebases. Persistence is a shared Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with a schema per bounded context; the reader endpoint is used for analytics-adjacent queries so we don't contend with write traffic.

  • Compute: ECS Fargate, one task definition per service, behind an internal ALB.
  • Data: Aurora PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ), Ecto for access, migrations gated in CI.
  • Infra as code: everything provisioned via AWS CDK — VPC, clusters, task definitions, and Aurora are all defined in the CDK app so environments (staging/prod) stay in lockstep.

Auth

There is no third-party auth broker. A small custom identity service issues short-lived JWTs on login; every other service validates the JWT signature locally (no per-request network hop) and trusts the sub claim as the player ID. Device-bound refresh tokens are stored in the identity service's own schema. Live-ops and quest mutations additionally require an internal service token — never a player JWT.

Services

ServiceResponsibilityDatastore
identityLogin, JWT issuance/rotation, device bindingAurora (schema: identity)
game_stateAuthoritative match/board state, progression, save reconciliationAurora (schema: state)
profilePlayer profile, inventory, wallet (coins/lives)Aurora (schema: profile)
questsQuest definitions, assignment, and completion trackingAurora (schema: quests)
live_opsEvent scheduling, feature-flag delivery, seasonal contentAurora (schema: liveops)

Endpoints & releasing

Phoenix serves a thin JSON API — no HTML, no channels here (realtime lives in Nakama). Routes are versioned under /api/v1 and health-checked at /healthz for the ALB. A representative controller and the release command:

elixir id}) do case Profile.get_player(id) do {:ok, player} -> json(conn, %{id: player.id, coins: player.coins, lives: player.lives}) {:error, :not_found} -> conn |> put_status(:not_found) |> json(%{error: "not_found"}) end end end # Build + run the release (baked into the Fargate image) # MIX_ENV=prod mix release harmony_backend # _build/prod/rel/harmony_backend/bin/harmony_backend start]]>

Migrations do not run on boot. Run bin/harmony_backend eval "HarmonyBackend.Release.migrate()" as a one-off Fargate task before rolling the services, so a bad migration can't take down every task at once.

Owner: Douglas. Ping in #engineering before schema changes to the shared Aurora cluster — profile and game_state both read the wallet columns.

record.title: Backend Services — Elixir/Phoenix
record.body:
This page describes the Elixir/Phoenix backend service, which sits behind Zombie Match 3D (listed as "Puzzles vs Zombies" until July 2025). Domino Delights ("Game of Dominoes"/GoD internally) runs a separate Node.js/Express service, and Combo Fighter its own Node/CDK stack - see "Runtime topology" below. The services own authoritative game state, player profiles, quests, and live-ops delivery. For the wider system picture and how these tie into Unity and Nakama, see Architecture Overview; teams, team chat and team leaderboards are documented separately in Nakama Server Setup & Operations.

Ownership is deliberately thin - a ten-person studio at this revision - seven paid staff plus three unpaid founders (down from a 2024 peak of 19 after the October 2025 reduction) can't staff a service mesh. Each title owns its own backend - all three were forked from the same AWS game-backend sample and allowed to diverge. Zombie Match 3D runs this Elixir/Phoenix app on Aurora; Domino Delights runs a separate Node.js/Express service on DynamoDB; Combo Fighter has its own Node/CDK stack, though its client also calls this Phoenix API. Prefer boring and observable over clever.

Runtime & deployment

This app is a single ordinary Mix project (:zombies_game), not an umbrella, released with mix release into one container image and run as one ECS Fargate service. Live-ops schedules run in-process on a Quantum cron inside that service; quests and identity are separate serverless stacks (see the table below)

  • Compute: ECS Fargate, one task definition per service, each behind its own public ALB (the Phoenix game API on prod-backend.zombies-game.com).
  • Data: Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 (a single serverless writer, no read replica), Ecto for access, migrations gated in CI.
  • Infra as code: everything provisioned via AWS CDK - VPC, clusters, task definitions, and Aurora are all defined in the CDK app so environments (dev/prod) stay in lockstep.

Auth

Auth is split, and the two halves are documented on different pages. Nakama owns accounts, friends and sessions (see Nakama Setup and the API reference); this Phoenix service does not issue tokens of its own - it verifies JWTs issued by our own identity service via a Joken JWKS strategy (aws_auth/verifier.ex; issuer read from the ISSUER_ENDPOINT environment variable in config/runtime.exs, JWKS at $ISSUER_ENDPOINT/.well-known/jwks.json, audience gamebackend). There is no third-party identity broker. The issuer is the AWS Game Backend Framework Custom Identity Component, deployed from our own CDK app (match3d-backend-auth): Python Lambdas behind API Gateway over DynamoDB, publishing an RS256 key set through CloudFront and rotating it weekly. Its CDK records the reason Cognito is not used - a cdk-nag suppression reading "The API cannot use Cognito User Pools as it is an API built for login and authentication for custom identities." The @moduledoc on verifier.ex still says "AWS Cognito JWT Joken strategy"; that string is inherited from the AWS sample and is stale. Short-lived JWTs are validated on login; every other service validates the JWT signature locally (no per-request network hop) and trusts the sub claim as the player ID. Device-bound refresh tokens are stored in the identity service's own schema. Live-ops and quest mutations additionally require an internal service token - never a player JWT.

Services

ServiceResponsibilityRuntimeDatastore
identityLogin, JWT issuance/rotation, device binding; federates Sign in with Apple on iOS and Google Play Games on Android, layered over anonymous guest identitiesPython Lambdas behind API Gateway (separate stack)DynamoDB
game_stateAuthoritative match/board state, progression, save reconciliationthis Phoenix serviceAurora
profilePlayer profile, inventory, wallet (coins/lives)this Phoenix serviceAurora
questsQuest definitions, assignment, and completion trackingNode Lambdas behind API Gateway (separate stack, shared across titles)DynamoDB
live_opsEvent scheduling and seasonal contentin-process Quantum cron in this servicereward tables authored in Google Sheets and imported on a schedule

Client feature flags and ad kill-switches are not in this service at all - they live in Firebase Remote Config and are read by the Unity client. Live-event enable flags are a separate thing and are compile-time literals in this service's config (see Live-Ops Event Engine).

Endpoints & releasing

Phoenix serves the JSON game API plus a LiveView admin surface (player browser, dashboard, login) mounted under the browser pipeline. Routes are served unversioned under /api and health-checked at /health for the ALB. A representative controller and the release command:

elixir id}) do case Profile.get_player(id) do {:ok, player} -> json(conn, %{id: player.id, coins: player.coins, lives: player.lives}) {:error, :not_found} -> conn |> put_status(:not_found) |> json(%{error: "not_found"}) end end end # Build + run the release (baked into the Fargate image) # MIX_ENV=prod mix release zombies_game # _build/prod/rel/zombies_game/bin/zombies_game start]]>

Migrations do not run on boot. Run bin/zombies_game eval "ZombiesGame.Release.migrate()" as a one-off Fargate task before rolling the services, so a bad migration can't take down every task at once.

record.title: Live-Ops Event Engine
record.body:
The Live-Ops Event Engine powers all recurring in-game events for Zombie Match 3D ("Puzzles vs Zombies" in stores). It defines, schedules, and fires timed content — Plague Race, Zombie Lane, Endless Monster Mode — and drives the associated leaderboards and lives economy. This page documents the architecture, the scheduler's known fragility, and the July 2025 outage that materially hit revenue. For upcoming cadence and slot ownership see Live-Ops Event Calendar & Planning.

Architecture

The engine has three cooperating parts. Event definitions are static config authored by design; the scheduler is the runtime that evaluates windows and fires state transitions; the leaderboard service ranks entries and settles rewards at event close.

ComponentResponsibilityOwner
Event definitionsDeclarative config: event type, reward table, start/end windows, cohort targetingDesign (Julia Lawson)
SchedulerRuns on hourly Quantum crons (0 * * * *); opens and closes events. Lives regeneration is not on this schedule.Backend (Douglas)
Leaderboard serviceIngests scores during a window, freezes and settles rewards at closeBackend

The lives coupling

A deliberate but risky decision: player life regeneration runs on the same scheduler tick loop as event firing. This keeps the timing model simple, but it means one failure mode takes down two player-facing systems at once. See the incident below.

Scheduler is a single point of failure. The scheduler runs as a supervised cluster-wide singleton, so a crashed process is restarted elsewhere; what it does not survive is a deploy that leaves the job unscheduled. If it stalls, live events stop firing and lives stop regenerating. Do not add new subsystems to the tick loop without a leader-election plan.

July 2025 outage

Between roughly Jul 12–26, 2025, the event/lives scheduler stopped advancing. The first player-visible symptom was lives no longer regenerating, first observed around 03:41 on Jul 13, 2025. No scheduled live events fired for the duration of the window, and store revenue dipped materially — on the order of 30% across the outage — as the core reason-to-return loop went dark. No standalone ticket was cut at the time; the timeline was reconstructed after the fact from warehouse metrics and scheduler logs.

The 30% revenue figure is coherence-locked to the BI warehouse. Treat the warehouse aggregation as the source of truth for the outage window; do not re-derive it from raw event logs, which are incomplete for those days.

Remediation

  • Add a heartbeat + external watchdog that pages on a missed scheduler tick (target: alert within 5 minutes, not 12+ hours).
  • Decouple life regeneration from event firing so a scheduler stall degrades one system, not both.
  • Introduce leader election so a second process can take over the tick loop.
  • Backfill a lives-regeneration reconciler that can catch a cohort up after a stall.
  • Dashboard the scheduler's last-tick timestamp alongside revenue so drift is visible on the same screen.

Design context for the coupled lives/event model and the related quest timing regression lives in Quest System — Design & Incident Postmortem.

record.title: Live-Ops Event Engine
record.body:
The Live-Ops Event Engine powers all recurring in-game events for Zombie Match 3D (listed as "Puzzles vs Zombies" until the July 2025 store rename). It defines, schedules, and fires timed content - Plague Race, Zombie Lane, Endless Monster Mode - and drives the associated leaderboards and lives economy. This page documents the architecture, the scheduler's known fragility, and the July 2025 outage that took Domino Delights live events dark - the record never marks it restored. For upcoming cadence and slot ownership see Live-Ops Event Calendar & Planning.

Architecture

The engine has three cooperating parts. Event definitions are reward tables authored by design in Google Sheets and hot-loaded by the backend; the scheduler is the runtime that evaluates windows and fires state transitions; the leaderboard service ranks entries and settles rewards at event close.

ComponentResponsibilityOwner
Event definitionsReward tables are authored in Google Sheets and imported hourly; windows are cron expressions baked into the CDK stack; there is no remote kill-switch for live events - Domino Delights gates them on a compiled client constant and Zombie Match 3D's per-event flags are literals in the backend runtime config, so turning an event on or off means a deploy or a direct database edit. There is no cohort-targeting field.Design (Julia Lawson)
SchedulerEach event type runs its own cron, all at 00:00 UTC - Plague Race, Endless Monster daily and Boss Arena daily; Leagues, Endless Monster weekly and Collect & Win weekly; Season Pass monthly on the 1st at 00:00 UTC (the CDK sets its schedule to 0 0 1 * * in production and the module is the monthly season-pass server); each season then runs to the start of the next month, which is the monthly window the Season Pass spec describes). The Quantum scheduler runs both: the four Google-Sheets reward importers (hourly in production) and every event-reset job - each leaderboard server registers its own Quantum job at boot from the cron string on its leaderboard row, so event firing and reward import share one scheduler. Lives regeneration is not on any of these.Backend (Douglas)
Leaderboard serviceIngests scores during a window, freezes and settles rewards at closeBackend

Lives regeneration

Life regeneration is computed client-side from server time and written back to the server; the server only clamps negative values. It is not on the scheduler and shares no failure domain with event firing - the two are independent. The July 2025 outage saw both symptoms at once, but that was co-occurrence: the stuck-lives reports are a separate, still-open client-side bug (ENG-2277, ENG-2400). See the incident below.

Scheduler has no leader: every node runs its own. The scheduler is a supervised in-process Quantum instance on EVERY node, not a cluster-wide singleton: jobs register with a node-local run strategy while production runs three Fargate tasks, so each event-reset cron currently fires once per task. A crashed process is restarted in place by its own supervisor; what it does not survive is a deploy that leaves the job unscheduled. A single stalled process does not stop event firing; what does is a deploy that leaves the job unscheduled on every node, which is how the July 2025 stall happened. Lives are unaffected - they are computed on the client. Do not add new subsystems to the tick loop without a leader-election plan.

July 2025 outage

From at least Jul 11, 2025 the event scheduler stopped advancing for Domino Delights, and no message anywhere in the record marks it restored. The same failure had happened a fortnight earlier and was cleared by hand. Lives are computed client-side (see above) and are not on the scheduler, so the stall could not stop the timer. The stuck-lives reports in the same thread are a separate, still-open bug (ENG-2277, ENG-2400) whose cause was never established. The lives write path stayed up throughout - backend granted manual lives top-ups on 14, 19 and 24 July while events were still not firing - and other accounts regenerated normally on the same build. The earliest symptom in the July thread is missing weekend events, reported on Jul 12, 2025 alongside a lives timer stuck at four. The 03:41 on Jul 13 figure is one reported player's lives balance beginning to fall in Metabase, not a first observation - a ticket relayed on Jul 12 said the problem had already been running for three days. Players reported seeing only two live events on the weekend, with River Rush, Streak Fever and Axe Arena not firing. It was not global - other accounts regenerated lives normally throughout - and no end date exists in the record: the same player's lives were broken again on Jul 24, coin balances were reported stuck negative on Jul 28, the same events-not-firing-until-someone-triggers-the-scheduler-by-hand failure was still being reported on Oct 27, and a lives-regeneration bug (ENG-2400) opened on Nov 2, 2025 was never closed. Zombie Match 3D was unaffected; its Plague Race ran normally that week. No standalone ticket was cut at the time; the timeline was reconstructed afterwards from support threads and scheduler logs.

Measure this outage from LIVE_EVENT_PERFORMANCE status and participation on Domino Delights, not from a revenue delta. Domino Delights revenue declined steadily across Jun-Jul 2025 as part of that title's wind-down, before, during and after the window; do not read that trend as outage impact.

Remediation

  • Add a heartbeat + external watchdog that pages on a missed scheduler tick (target: alert within 5 minutes, not 12+ hours).
  • Monitor the lives write-back route independently of scheduler ticks, so two co-occurring symptoms in different failure domains can be told apart on the first day rather than the third.
  • Introduce leader election so each cron fires once cluster-wide instead of once per Fargate task (Quantum.RunStrategy.Global, or an external lock).
  • Build a repro harness for ENG-2277 / ENG-2400 - every reported case was cleared only by a manual backend lives grant, and no fix was ever shipped.
  • Dashboard the scheduler's last-tick timestamp alongside revenue so drift is visible on the same screen.

Design context for the lives and event-timing models and the related quest timing regression lives in Quest System - Design & Incident Postmortem.

The single-scheduler design has bothered me since we shipped it. Twelve-plus hours with no alert is the real failure here - the stall itself is recoverable, but nobody knew until revenue told us. Watchdog + heartbeat should jump ahead of leader election on the list; it's a fraction of the effort and covers the worst case.

Agreed, Arthur Blake. I've reordered remediation so the heartbeat + external watchdog is first. Decoupling lives from event firing is the bigger refactor but it's what actually stops one stall from becoming two outages - I'll scope that after the watchdog lands.
